chapters.title: Chapter 5: Where Kelly Breaks Down, and Putting It Together

lessons.title: Common Overbetting Mistakes That Blow Up Traders Who Know Kelly

children.text: Knowing the Kelly formula does not prevent overbetting. Most traders who blow up despite understanding Kelly aren't ignoring it; they're applying it to the wrong numbers, at the wrong moment, or without noticing the numbers have quietly gone stale. This lesson catalogs five specific ways that happens.
Mistake 1: Trading Full Kelly "Because the Math Said So"

Chapter 3 covered this in depth: full Kelly carries a 50% chance of a 50% drawdown even when every input is exactly correct. Traders who understand the formula but skip the fractional-Kelly adjustment are betting the growth-maximizing fraction while ignoring the one result, from Lesson 3.1, that explains why almost nobody actually trades it.

f* = μ/σ² from Lesson 2.3 uses current volatility, not the volatility that happened to prevail when the position was first sized. Volatility is not stable: it clusters, and it spikes sharply around known event risk such as Union Budget day, election results, or a surprise RBI policy move. A trader who sizes once during a calm period and never revisits σ walks straight into an oversized position exactly when it matters most.

Illustrative example: a trader sizes a Nifty position using a calm-market volatility estimate of 14% and an assumed 8% expected excess return, then holds that same size straight through an event window where realized volatility doubles to 28%.

body.caption: A memorable rule: every time volatility doubles, the correct Kelly fraction falls to a quarter of what it was

body.text: Running 4x the currently-correct fraction is not a mild overshoot. Lesson 3.1 showed that growth turns negative once a position exceeds roughly 2x the true full-Kelly fraction. This trader isn't a bit too aggressive; they are deep in the territory where the formula itself predicts capital destruction, using an input that was accurate a week ago and is wrong today.

children.text: Mistake 3: Adding Correlated Positions One at a Time

Lessons 4.3 and 4.4 showed that correlated positions need to be sized jointly, using Σ⁻¹μ, not added up individually. In practice this mistake rarely happens as one deliberate decision. It happens position by position through a trading day or week: a Nifty futures trade in the morning, a correlated bank stock in the afternoon, an index call option the next day, each one individually small and each one individually "within budget." None of them get checked against what is already held, and the combined exposure quietly ends up far past what a joint calculation would allow.
Mistake 4: Doubling Down Instead of Updating

A losing streak is data. Lessons 1.2 and 3.3 built the tools to ask whether a run of losses is still consistent with the win rate a system was sized on, or whether it's evidence that win rate has changed. Instead, a common instinct is to treat a losing streak as "due for a win" and increase size to recover faster, the opposite of what the evidence supports.

body.label: P(2 or fewer wins in 12 trades, if the true win rate really is 55%)
body.context: Roughly a 1-in-125 event under the original assumption. A losing streak this extreme should trigger a re-check of p, not a bigger bet to catch up.

body.text: This doesn't mean every losing streak signals a broken edge; short losing streaks are entirely normal even for a genuinely 55%-win-rate system. What it means is that a streak this improbable under the original assumption is worth investigating using Lesson 1.2's confidence-interval tools, not treated as bad luck that justifies a bigger bet to compensate for.

children.text: Mistake 5: Trading a Backtest That Has Gone Stale

An edge measured two or three years ago is not guaranteed to still exist today. Market regimes shift, a once-obscure setup can get crowded once enough traders and screeners find it, and regulatory or structural changes can quietly erode what a backtest captured. Sizing today's trades off yesterday's win rate, without ever re-validating on fresh, out-of-sample data, is estimation error of a different kind than Lesson 3.3 covered: not "the sample was too small," but "the sample no longer describes the present." The fix is the same discipline from Chapter 3, applied on a rolling basis rather than once: periodically re-check p and b against recent, out-of-sample trades, not just the original backtest.

body.title: Diagnose the trader
body.scenario: A trader sized a Nifty options position using a 15% volatility estimate calculated three months ago and has not updated it since, including through last week's RBI policy announcement, which sharply increased realized volatility. Separately, over the same period, they added two more positions in stocks that move closely with Nifty, each one individually small relative to their account.
body.prompt: Which two mistakes from this lesson is this trader making? Explain briefly.
body.modelAnswer: This trader is making Mistake 2 (sizing off yesterday's volatility, since the σ estimate is three months stale and specifically wasn't updated through a known event that raised volatility) and Mistake 3 (adding correlated positions one at a time, since the new stocks move closely with Nifty and were each added without checking the combined exposure against the existing position). Both mistakes can look individually reasonable in the moment while combining into a position that is far more concentrated and far more oversized than either mistake alone would suggest.

body.title: The volatility-doubling rule
body.question: If volatility triples (not doubles) while μ stays the same, what happens to f* = μ/σ²?
options: It falls to a third of its original value
It falls to a ninth of its original value
It stays the same, since only σ changed
It triples, since the formula includes σ
body.explanation: f* = μ/σ². Since σ enters squared, tripling σ means σ² increases ninefold, so f* falls to 1/9 of its original value. The relationship between volatility and Kelly fraction is quadratic, not linear, which is exactly why stale volatility estimates are so dangerous.

points: Full Kelly, uncoordinated correlated position-adding, and stale inputs, whether volatility, win-rate estimates, or an aging backtest, cause most real-world overbetting, not ignorance of the formula itself.
Volatility is squared in f* = μ/σ², so a doubling of volatility quarters the correct fraction; sizing off stale σ is especially dangerous around known event risk.
Correlated positions added incrementally through a trading day or week can combine into far more exposure than any single trade suggests, unless checked jointly.

A losing streak that is statistically very unlikely under your assumed win rate, roughly under 1% probability in this lesson's example, is evidence to re-check your estimate, not a signal to bet bigger to catch up.
An edge that was genuinely real when first backtested can decay over time; sizing discipline needs to include periodic re-validation, not just a one-time calculation.
